record.original_question: For a preemptive uniprocessor real-time system modeled as a constrained-deadline sporadic task system tau, where each task tau_i = (C_i, D_i, T_i) has relative deadline D_i no larger than its period T_i, determine whether there exists a pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm for deciding Earliest Deadline First schedulability. Earliest Deadline First scheduling always executes the pending job with the earliest deadline, and tau is EDF-schedulable when EDF meets all deadlines for every legal sequence of job arrivals. The source records that weak coNP-hardness is known, leaving the pseudo-polynomial-time decision question open.

evidence.quote: The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm schedules at each instant in time the job currently awaiting execution that has the earliest deadline.

Problem 2 (Computational complexity of uniprocessor EDF-schedulability analysis – constrained-deadline tasks.) What is the computational complexity of the following problem? Input: Constrained-deadline sporadic task system τ Question: Is τ EDF-schedulable?

Progress since Dagstuhl. Problem 2 was shown to be weakly coNP-hard by Eisenbrand and Rothvoß in [9]. The outstanding open question is thus whether a pseudo-polynomial time algorithm exists for problem 2.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a preemptive uniprocessor real-time system specified by a constrained-deadline sporadic task system τ = {τ_1, …, τ_n}. Each task τ_i = (C_i, D_i, T_i) consists of a worst-case execution requirement C_i ∈ ℤ_{>0}, a relative deadline D_i ∈ ℤ_{>0}, and a minimum inter-arrival separation (period) T_i ∈ ℤ_{>0}, subject to C_i ≤ D_i ≤ T_i. A task τ_i releases an (a priori unbounded) sequence of jobs: each released job has execution requirement at most C_i, and two consecutive jobs of τ_i are released at least T_i time units apart; a job released at time r has absolute deadline r + D_i. The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduler is the on-line preemptive scheduler that, at each instant, executes the pending job with the smallest absolute deadline (ties broken arbitrarily). The system τ is EDF-schedulable if, for every legal sequence of job arrivals consistent with the parameters above, EDF completes every job by its absolute deadline. 

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a constrained-deadline sporadic task system τ (with all parameters encoded in binary), decides whether τ is EDF-schedulable and runs in time bounded by a polynomial in n and in the largest numerical parameter max_i max{C_i, D_i, T_i} (i.e., a pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm)? Equivalently, exhibit such an algorithm or prove that none exists (e.g., by establishing strong coNP-hardness).
artifact.status_search_result: The exact computational complexity of EDF-schedulability for constrained-deadline sporadic task systems on a uniprocessor remains open. Weak coNP-hardness is known (Eisenbrand–Rothvoß), and processor-demand analysis gives pseudo-polynomial algorithms only under bounded-utilization assumptions; no general pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm or strong coNP-hardness proof has been reported as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: A Closer Look at Pseudo-polynomial Time and Its Use in Real-Time Scheduling Theory
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses pseudo-polynomial time schedulability tests and ongoing efforts to extend them.
status_evidence.claim: Pseudo-polynomial schedulability remains a focus of ongoing research with results only under restricted assumptions.

status_evidence.title: EDF-schedulability of synchronous periodic task systems is coNP-hard
status_evidence.snippet: Eisenbrand and Rothvoß show weak coNP-hardness of EDF schedulability for constrained-deadline systems.
status_evidence.claim: Only weak coNP-hardness is known; pseudo-polynomial-time decidability is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Constant Bandwidth Servers with Constrained Deadlines
status_evidence.snippet: Processor demand analysis is pseudo-polynomial only when utilization is bounded away from 1.
status_evidence.claim: Existing pseudo-polynomial algorithms apply only under bounded-utilization assumptions, not in general.
